Hypothesis Bayes Factors

Source: R/hypothesis.R
hypothesis.Rd

Computes Bayes factors for scalar hypotheses written as expressions, for example "mu = 0", "year > 0", or "mu_alloc[alternate] > mu_alloc[random]".

Usage

hypothesis(object, ...)

# Default S3 method
hypothesis(object, hypothesis, ...)

# S3 method for class 'brma'
hypothesis(
  object,
  hypothesis,
  component = "auto",
  standardized_coefficients = FALSE,
  conditional = FALSE,
  logBF = FALSE,
  BF01 = FALSE,
  seed = NULL,
  density_method = "qCMDE",
  density_control = NULL,
  n_samples = 10000,
  columns = "default",
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'marginal_means.brma'
hypothesis(
  object,
  hypothesis,
  parameter = NULL,
  logBF = FALSE,
  BF01 = FALSE,
  seed = NULL,
  density_method = NULL,
  density_control = NULL,
  columns = "default",
  ...
)

bf_hypothesis(object, ...)

BF_hypothesis(object, ...)

Arguments

object

a fitted brma, BMA, RoBMA, or a posterior object accepted by BayesTools::hypothesis_BF().

...

additional arguments passed to methods. For fitted brma objects, unused arguments trigger a warning.

hypothesis

character vector with scalar hypothesis statements. For marginal_means.brma objects, constants are specified on the fitted linear-predictor scale, even when the object stores a display transformation. Separate statements may reference different model parameters, also the marginal means of different parameters of marginal_means.brma objects (unless parameter is set); each statement itself must resolve to one scalar model target.

component

parameter component. Defaults to "auto", which infers the component when possible. Use "mods" (alias "location"), "scale", or "random" to disambiguate terms used in multiple model components. A statement whose references still name several model parameters stops with an error of class BayesTools_hypothesis_ambiguous, with the parent class BayesTools_hypothesis_statement: the statement or component needs to change, the test itself is not unavailable. An ambiguous reference that BayesTools refuses with the class BayesTools_parameter_ambiguous (for example the contrast coefficient "g{1}" of a factor term in the location and the scale formula) has these classes too, before its BayesTools classes. A statement whose parameters belong to another component than component, including a name that is known only outside component next to references of component (with or without factor levels, e.g. "log_tau_g[a] > mu_g[a]" with component = "mods"), stops with the classes BayesTools_hypothesis_statement and BayesTools_hypothesis_component_mismatch (plot.brma() stops with RoBMA_component_mismatch for its own component mismatches). The exception is the alias of a factor term of both the location and the scale formula (for example g for mods = ~ g, scale = ~ g) next to a name that is unknown within component, such as a name of the other component or a display label (for example "g > log_tau_intercept" with component = "mods"): the statement is resolved without component, where the alias is ambiguous, and stops with BayesTools_hypothesis_statement followed by the classes of the BayesTools refusal of its first unresolved reference, the ambiguity of the alias (BayesTools_parameter_ambiguous, without BayesTools_hypothesis_ambiguous, as component is set already) or the unknown name (BayesTools_parameter_not_found, for example in "log_tau_intercept < g" or, with a level of the alias, in "g[a] > log_tau_intercept"). The display labels of the summary tables (for example "(mu) intercept", "exp(intercept)", or "(mu) g[a]") name the parameters they label, with and without component. The random component supports point, interval, and directional hypotheses for semantic standard deviation, variance, correlation, and allocation quantities. Point-null hypotheses require a direct parameter reference, a factor level, or a linear combination of the levels of one factor term (for example "g[a] = g[b]" or "2 * g[a] = 0.1"). Point hypotheses on a random-effect variance are evaluated through its standard deviation, so that both give the same Bayes factor at positive variance values. At zero, the square map is singular: the variance is tested on its own scale and follows its own prior-ordinate eligibility rules. A statement comparing such a point with a region of the variance (for example "tau2 = 0.09 vs tau2 > 0.09") evaluates the point through the standard deviation and the region on the variance draws. Certified exp(affine) fitted-scale hypotheses are available with KDE only for atom-free, unconditional scalar targets. Values at a prior point mass (for example, gated components at 0) have no Savage-Dickey Bayes factor; the Component Inclusion table compares the exclusion and inclusion of gated components. Point nulls at an exact support boundary (for example, a variance proportion at 0) use the one-sided prior ordinate when BayesTools classifies it as exact, finite, and positive. Publication-bias parameters are not supported (class BayesTools_hypothesis_target), including the quantities of the publication-bias prior such as the weight-function coordinates "omega[0,0.025]" and "bias_indicator". Other quantities of the fitted model that are no tested model parameter, such as inclusion indicators ("mu_x_indicator"), the component inclusions of variance allocations ("inclusion(study)"), or latent cluster effects, are refused with the class BayesTools_hypothesis_target as well; hypothesis_quantities() lists the tested quantities.

standardized_coefficients

whether moderator and scale coefficients are tested on the standardized predictor scale. Defaults to FALSE.

conditional

whether to use the conditional posterior for product-space model-averaging objects. Defaults to FALSE. When this argument is omitted and the selected parameter has both null and alternative components, a warning notes that the full ensemble is used. Pass FALSE explicitly to retain that test without the warning, or TRUE to test only models where the parameter is active. Point hypotheses on linear combinations of factor levels of model-averaged objects require conditional = TRUE: the levels share the null component of the averaged prior.

logBF

whether to display the Bayes factor on the log scale.

BF01

whether to display the inverse Bayes factor.

seed

optional seed used by BayesTools for sampled prior quantities.

density_method

posterior density method. Defaults to "qCMDE" for fitted brma objects. "KDE" uses the standard BayesTools kernel density estimate. "normal" uses the BayesTools normal approximation for point-null hypotheses on fitted brma objects. "qCMDE" and "IWMDE" attach RoBMA likelihood-aware posterior ordinates for point-null hypotheses and propagate their BF_error estimates printed as error%(BF). BF_error is a Monte Carlo diagnostic for the computed posterior ordinate, not a complete standard error. For a subsampled mixed posterior it is a worst-correlation delta upper bound combining the selected active-row and complete indicator-chain components. It excludes uncertainty in the prior ordinate and, for IWMDE, uncertainty from estimating the conditional weight function. At a location that is also a posterior atom, qCMDE/IWMDE reports the continuous ordinate; the atom probability is a separate discrete mass. Use density_diagnostics() to inspect the attached computation and reliability diagnostics. For marginal_means.brma objects, "normal" is not supported. Their default NULL reuses the density method stored by marginal_means(); explicitly request "KDE" to override it. "qCMDE" and "IWMDE" compute missing point-null ordinates from the stored source model. Matching is case-insensitive. qCMDE/IWMDE ordinates use the exact fitted-to-original structural coefficient map and induced prior density stored by BayesTools. qCMDE/IWMDE supports exact linear maps: coefficients, factor levels of every contrast, and linear combinations of levels. For nonlinear joint maps, such as an exponentiated intercept that also depends on varying slopes, KDE point and directional hypotheses are available only when structural metadata certifies an atom-free, unconditional scalar target and the point is inside the open transformed support. Alternatively, use standardized_coefficients = TRUE.

The statements are planned and evaluated by the hypothesis engine of BayesTools (BayesTools::hypothesis_BF_model()); RoBMA describes its models to it (BayesTools::hypothesis_provider()) and provides the density methods qCMDE and IWMDE (BayesTools::hypothesis_density_backend()). Every statement is planned before it is evaluated: the plan records the tested target (its weights on the fitted coefficients, its BayesTools prior density and declared atoms), the classification of each point value by BayesTools::prior_ordinate_status(), and whether each density method can evaluate it; hypothesis_quantities() renders the same plans. A point hypothesis whose prior ordinate is not exact, finite, and regular stops with the BayesTools condition class (for example BayesTools_point_mass_at_null, BayesTools_infinite_ordinate, or BayesTools_inexact_ordinate). Other refusals of a test that cannot be computed have the class BayesTools_hypothesis_unavailable and one of BayesTools_hypothesis_fixed (the quantity is fixed by the fitted model), BayesTools_hypothesis_target (no supported target or prior density), or BayesTools_hypothesis_method (the density method is unavailable for the target); linear combinations that BayesTools cannot certify keep the class BayesTools_linear_target_unavailable. A method refusal because the fitted model does not support qCMDE/IWMDE also has the classes of the refusals of these requests by plot.brma() and marginal_means(): RoBMA_density_method_unavailable and one class naming the cause, RoBMA_density_method_random_unknown_v (brma.mv() random-formula models without known V), RoBMA_density_method_scale_components (component-specific scale formulas), or RoBMA_density_method_glmm (IWMDE for binomial and Poisson GLMMs). qCMDE/IWMDE refusals for a cause for which plot.brma() refuses these methods have its classes too: RoBMA_density_method_conditional_random (conditional random-effect statements), RoBMA_density_method_random_target (random-effect quantities without a supported scalar random-component coordinate), and RoBMA_density_method_original_scale (original-scale coefficients whose fitted map is nonlinear, such as exp(affine) targets). As in plot.brma(), allocated component SDs in a predictor-scaled block require standardized_coefficients = TRUE or density_method = 'KDE'; the block-wide restriction also covers an unchanged centered intercept. As in plot.brma(), the capability of the fitted model is checked before these causes and before other qCMDE/IWMDE refusals of the tested quantity: a request to which both apply stops with the capability refusal. A qCMDE/IWMDE ordinate that cannot be constructed stops with RoBMA_density_ordinate_error; when a fitted chain has no eligible row of the target, the error also has the class RoBMA_density_chain_coverage and its message names density_method = "KDE" and longer chains as remedies. The refusal for fewer than 20 continuous active samples of the target takes precedence over this diagnosis: such a target is refused for that reason alone, without the class RoBMA_density_chain_coverage, even when a fitted chain has none of its rows.

Statements that need to be restated, or an argument that needs to change, stop with the class BayesTools_hypothesis_statement without BayesTools_hypothesis_unavailable: point expressions that are no direct reference (for example "2 * mu = 0"), nonlinear expressions of factor levels, several point values of a random-effect variance in one statement, one quantity named by several names in one statement (for example "mu > 0 & intercept < 1" or "g[a] > mu_g[a]"; use one name), model-averaged marginal-means statements that mix point and region events or span several marginal means (levels or scalar marginal means), ambiguous references (BayesTools_hypothesis_ambiguous, see component), references to parameters of another component (BayesTools_hypothesis_component_mismatch), marginal-means statements that refer to another parameter than parameter (BayesTools_hypothesis_parameter_mismatch), factor contrast coefficients such as "g{1}" (state the hypothesis on factor levels; a selector of a coefficient that is a level, such as "g{1}" of a treatment factor, also has the classes of the BayesTools refusal BayesTools_selector_unavailable, which names the level), references to unknown names or factor levels, and statements that reference no parameter (followed by the classes of the BayesTools refusal of such a statement, BayesTools_hypothesis_no_parameters and BayesTools_parameter_resolution_error, on fitted objects and on marginal means). An unknown name or level also has the classes BayesTools_parameter_not_found and BayesTools_parameter_resolution_error, with which BayesTools refuses it (on fitted objects and in linear combinations of marginal-means levels, the BayesTools condition itself with its fields alias and available). Every other refusal of a statement's references by BayesTools (class BayesTools_parameter_resolution_error) stops hypothesis() too, on fitted objects and on marginal means, as the BayesTools condition with its classes and fields after BayesTools_hypothesis_statement, also when BayesTools raises it only when it evaluates the statement (for example the whole factor term next to one of its levels, "g[a] > mu_g", as an unknown quantity). Missing or unsupported fitted metadata of the tested target (a parameter catalog without RoBMA parameters, the coefficient transform, the fitted coordinates, or the linear weights of a factor level; a fit of an older RoBMA/BayesTools build) stop with the class RoBMA_refit_required: refit the model. Its parent BayesTools_refit_required is the class of every error of RoBMA and BayesTools that asks for a refit; BayesTools' own refit errors stop hypothesis() unconverted.

density_control

named list of qCMDE/IWMDE tuning settings. Supported entries are n_points (default 100), samples (the fixed posterior-row sample size, default 500 for qCMDE and 1000 for IWMDE; use Inf for the eligible-row census), target_relative_mcse (default 0.05), normalization_points (default NULL, resolved to max(50, n_points)), normalization_prob (default 0.999; lower than 1 for qCMDE), and display_grid (default "adaptive"). integration_control (default NULL) retains the fitted selection-integration settings. Supply a control created by set_selection_likelihood_control() to change those settings for this post-fit calculation, for example list(integration_control = set_selection_likelihood_control(max_points_per_scramble = 32768)). This entry is available for Gaussian selection models with a fitted integration plan. The fitted object and posterior draws are unchanged. The maximum point budget controls factor QMC fallback; analytic and deterministic quadrature rules remain unchanged. Point ordinates use one state-independent simple random sample selected before ordinate contributions are evaluated. Multiple direct scalar point ordinates for one target share the same conditional-normalization pass while retaining separate diagnostics. A finite estimate is returned independently of its sample diagnostics. If the fixed sample does not meet the precision target, a warning recommends increasing samples or using the census; if the census does not meet the target, obtain more posterior draws. display_grid is immaterial for point-only requests. qCMDE normalizes each posterior row's conditional density over a range covering at least its central normalization_prob mass, on normalization_points nodes and the nested grid of those nodes and their midpoints. The mass of a row left outside the range, its truncation \(t\), is therefore at most 1 - normalization_prob: zero for rows whose Gaussian likelihood kernel meets a normal prior and whose evaluated values are those of the resulting truncated normal (their normalizer is its closed-form mass, so no lattice decides it), exactly computed for such rows that keep the lattice normalizer, bounded for a Gaussian kernel with another proper scalar prior, and estimated from the tails (each tail extended until its estimate is at most (1 - normalization_prob) / 2) otherwise. The tail extension has a limit, ends at values the joint density cannot evaluate, and cannot help a tail that does not decay, so the estimate for such a row can exceed that target and the bound below with it. A row normalizer missing the fraction \(t\) overstates that row's density by the factor \(1 / (1 - t)\), so the ordinate is overstated by at most \(t / (1 - t)\) for the largest row truncation, which is at most (1 - normalization_prob) / normalization_prob; at the default 0.999 that is about 0.1 percent, and it is attained when all rows share one conditional law. density_diagnostics() report the largest row truncation (normalization_truncation), how it is known (normalization_truncation_status), and this bound (truncation_ordinate_bound), together with the change between the two nested grids (ordinate_relative_change), which estimates the discretization error of the lattice normalizers, and the contribution-share weighted lattice-resolution estimate (lattice_resolution_relative_error). The resolution estimate uses the Gaussian kernel width at the nested-grid maximum, or local log curvature when no kernel is available. Neither the resolution component nor the combined error estimate is a rigorous bound; a sharp prior core can be narrower than its likelihood kernel. Exact nonlattice normalizers have no lattice-resolution component. Set normalization_prob closer to 1 to reduce the truncation, and increase normalization_points to reduce the discretization. IWMDE checks its normalization mass on normalization_points points over the central normalization_prob quantile range of the target draws, widened by 10 percent on each side. A point ordinate warns at relative MCSE at least 5 percent, ESS below 100, maximum contribution share at least 20 percent, or fewer than 100 finite contributions. These same-sample diagnostics do not suppress a finite fixed-design estimate. The qCMDE ordinate error estimate (nested-grid change, lattice resolution and the tail-truncation bound) warns above 2.5 percent and is rejected above 5 percent; IWMDE normalization error warns above 5 percent and is rejected above 10 percent. For retained-location conditional normalizers, adaptive-quadrature sensitivity warns above 2.5 percent and is rejected above 5 percent.

n_samples

number of prior samples/grid points used by BayesTools for deterministic marginal prior densities.

columns

output columns passed to BayesTools::hypothesis_BF(). "default" returns the compact BayesTools table with Alternative, Null, BF, and error%(BF) columns. "all" also returns prior, posterior, and method columns. The prior and posterior columns are diagnostics rather than probabilities for all hypothesis types.

parameter

optional marginal-means parameter/term used to disambiguate the hypothesis expression. Without it, each statement is tested on the marginal means of the parameter it names, so that separate statements may refer to different parameters (for example c("g[a] > 0", "h[b] > 0")); the rows are those of the statements tested one at a time, in the order of the statements. One statement must refer to the marginal means of one parameter: a statement that names several (for example "g[a] > h[b]"), or an alias that names several parameters, stops with an error of class BayesTools_hypothesis_ambiguous, with the parent class BayesTools_hypothesis_statement; parameter selects the parameter of an ambiguous alias. With parameter, every statement is tested on that parameter, and a statement that refers to the marginal means of another parameter stops with an error of class BayesTools_hypothesis_parameter_mismatch, with the parent class BayesTools_hypothesis_statement; for a statement that names several parameters ("g[a] > h[b]" with parameter = "g") its message is the one given without parameter. A statement that references no marginal-means parameter stops with the class BayesTools_hypothesis_statement; for a statement without parameter symbols (for example "1 > 0", also with parameter) also with BayesTools_hypothesis_no_parameters and BayesTools_parameter_resolution_error, and for an unknown name, or an unknown level of a factor term, also with BayesTools_parameter_not_found and BayesTools_parameter_resolution_error, as on fitted objects.

Value

A BayesTools_hypothesis_BF BayesTools table.

Details

For a continuous focal parameter \(\theta\), nuisance parameters \(\xi\), and an unnormalized joint posterior kernel \(q(\theta,\xi)\), qCMDE estimates the posterior ordinate as $$\widehat{p}_{Q}(\theta^{*}\mid y)=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S} \frac{q(\theta^{*},\xi_{i})}{\int_{\Theta} q(t,\xi_{i})\,dt}.$$ Each row is therefore normalized over the focal-parameter support before the conditional densities are averaged. IWMDE instead uses $$\widehat{p}_{I}(\theta^{*}\mid y)=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S} w(\theta_{i}\mid\xi_{i})\frac{q(\theta^{*},\xi_{i})} {q(\theta_{i},\xi_{i})},$$ where \(w(\theta\mid\xi)\) is a normalized, fitted conditional weight. For half-bounded targets, IWMDE fits the distance from the declared boundary and normalizes a Normal weight over its central 95 percent positive-tail interval, using the actual computed endpoints. A draw outside that compact interval contributes zero while retaining its original row and chain. The same compact family is used when conditional fitting is unavailable. Compact focal support does not certify a finite joint second moment or MCMC long-run variance; reported uncertainty is conditional on the fitted proposal and does not include uncertainty from learning it on the same draws. Spike-mixture and product-space results additionally retain the posterior mass of the continuous active branch. These estimators build on conditional marginal density estimation and importance-weighted marginal density estimation (Gelfand et al. 1992; Chen 1994) .

qCMDE is the preferred likelihood-aware method when it is supported and its additional numerical normalization cost is acceptable. IWMDE can be faster, but is more sensitive to the adequacy and concentration of its fitted conditional weights. The normal approximation is useful as a rough check for near-normal interior ordinates; it is not a validation reference for skewed tails, bounded parameters, or one-sided support boundaries. Selected weightfunction models near zero cumulative ordered effects can take more than 10 minutes with qCMDE or IWMDE. qCMDE is the default for fitted brma objects. Use "KDE", "normal", or "IWMDE" explicitly to select another route. For binomial and Poisson GLMMs, the nuisance state includes the sampled estimate-level heterogeneity effects and baserates or log-rates. Averaging the normalized row-conditional focal densities over the posterior draws of this nuisance state targets the marginal posterior density by an exact identity; the estimate approximates that expectation with the posterior draws and numerical normalization, subject to the reported diagnostics. IWMDE is unavailable for GLMM density estimation because its high-dimensional conditional weights did not meet bridge-sampling certification. GLMM density curves and point-null hypotheses require qCMDE. qCMDE and IWMDE evaluate one scale formula: they are unavailable for brma.mv() models with component-specific scale formulas (a named scale list, e.g. one scale formula per random component), whose point-null hypotheses use density_method = "KDE".

For an unrestricted alternative against \(\theta=\theta_0\), the Savage-Dickey identity (Dickey 1971; Wagenmakers et al. 2010) gives \(BF_{10}=p(\theta_0\mid H_1)/p(\theta_0\mid y,H_1)\) only when the null model's nuisance-parameter prior is the conditional prior induced by the unrestricted model at \(\theta_0\). Otherwise, fit the constrained model separately and compare marginal likelihoods, for example by bridge sampling.

Marginal-means hypotheses are specified on the fitted linear-predictor scale. Display transformations stored by marginal_means() do not transform hypothesis constants. Single-model hypotheses and model-averaged region hypotheses use averaged marginal draws. Model-averaged point-null hypotheses use alternative-conditioned draws to avoid null atoms in averaged marginals. For model-averaged objects, hypotheses that mix point and region events, and point hypotheses on more than one marginal mean (several levels of a factor, or levels and scalar marginal means of one parameter or of several), are not supported. Separate region statements may refer to different parameters, while each statement refers to the marginal means of one parameter. Single-model hypotheses use one common averaged posterior and may combine these events. Point hypotheses require the exact prior ordinate that BayesTools attaches to the marginal mean, as for fitted objects.

References

Chen M (1994). “Importance-weighted marginal Bayesian posterior density estimation.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, 89(427), 818–824. doi:10.1080/01621459.1994.10476815 .

Dickey JM (1971). “The weighted likelihood ratio, linear hypotheses on normal location parameters.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 204–223. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177693507 .

Gelfand AE, Smith AF, Lee T (1992). “Bayesian analysis of constrained parameter and truncated data problems using Gibbs sampling.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, 87(418), 523–532. doi:10.1080/01621459.1992.10475235 .

Wagenmakers E, Lodewyckx T, Kuriyal H, Grasman R (2010). “Bayesian hypothesis testing for psychologists: A tutorial on the Savage–Dickey method.” Cognitive Psychology, 60(3), 158–189. doi:10.1016/j.cogpsych.2009.12.001 .

See also

density_diagnostics(), marginal_means(), plot.brma(), bridge_sampler.brma()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
fit <- brma(
  yi      = c(0.12, 0.20, 0.05, 0.33, 0.18),
  sei     = c(0.10, 0.12, 0.09, 0.15, 0.11),
  measure = "GEN"
)

# Average-effect hypotheses
hypothesis(fit, "mu != 0 vs mu = 0")
hypothesis(fit, "mu > 0 vs mu = 0")
hypothesis(fit, "mu > 0 vs mu < 0")

# Heterogeneity hypothesis
hypothesis(fit, "tau = 0 vs tau > 0", component = "scale")

dat <- data.frame(
  yi    = c(0.12, 0.20, 0.05, 0.33, 0.18, 0.41),
  sei   = c(0.10, 0.12, 0.09, 0.15, 0.11, 0.14),
  group = factor(c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"))
)
fit_mod <- brma(
  yi      = yi,
  sei     = sei,
  mods    = ~ group,
  data    = dat,
  measure = "GEN"
)

# Marginal-mean hypothesis for a factor level
emm <- marginal_means(fit_mod, density_method = "qCMDE")
hypothesis(emm, "group[B] > 0 vs group[B] = 0")
} # }
